definition: Token burn is spending far more tokens than a task deserved. It happens with vague prompts that need lots of back-and-forth, long pasted documents the model barely uses, or an agentic loop spinning its wheels. The tokens are real, the bill is real, and the value often isn't.

edges.label: see it happen
edges.note: DeepSeek's prompt-journey panel shows exactly where tokens get spent.

example.body: Someone pastes a 60-page PDF and writes “summarize this??” The model reads all 60 pages (huge input), isn't sure what's wanted, and produces a cautious 2,000-word summary covering everything (huge output). A sharper prompt — “summarize the pricing section in 5 bullets” — would have cost a tenth as much and been more useful.
example.title: The $12 “summarize this”

footnotes.body: Burn concentrates in output tokens (priced higher than input) and in reasoning traces for reasoning models. Mitigations: prompt specificity, retrieval instead of full-context pasting, iteration budgets on agentic loops, and tracking tokens-per-task in evals.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: Token Burn
tagline: When a vague prompt or a stuck loop spends far more tokens — and money — than the answer was worth.
whyItMatters: This is the number-one reason AI bills surprise people. Nothing is broken — the system did exactly what it was asked, just inefficiently. Learning to spot burn is learning to use AI cheaply.
